newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia metal's push for independence may founder.
newsitem.headline: Russia metal's push for independence may founder.

text.p: Russian metal producers' hopes of loosening ties with major western trading houses are likely to be dashed on the rocks of cash shortages and high borrowing costs, traders and analysts said on Thursday.

Russia's giant smelters said on Wednesday they wanted to reduce their dependence on tolling deals under which they take metal ores from international traders, process them and give them back to the traders for export on to world markets.

"The aluminium industry of Russia is now so integrated with the western trading system that I think these tolling arrangements will continue," said Boris Arlyuk, an independent analyst based in St Petersburg.
Analysts say tolling deals have saved cash-strapped metal producers from going bust during Russia's traumatic shift away from centralised support towards a market economy.
Russia's giant metal plants have been unable to raise cash to buy raw materials and have instead relied on tolling, which does not require upfront cash payments for supplies.
While Russian producers now want less tolling and, consequently, a bigger slice of hard currency earnings on refined metal sales, they are unlikely to find the cash to do so.

"I think the current (tolling) system will continue simply on the basis that the Russian base metal smelters do not have much (financial) leverage," said Raj Kohli of Paribas Capital Markets in London.
The stakes are high. The Russian metals export business was worth $16 billion in 1996, according to the chairman of the Association of Russian Metal Exporters, Vsevolod Generalov.
Some analysts say tolling alone is a $2 billion-a-year business for the Western commodities houses that provide ores and concentrates.
Lending rates in Russia are a sky-high 60 percent or so a year, but western trading firms can borrow money at around 12 percent, according to Arlyuk.
"On average (Russian) smelters only have around half the working capital they need to process ores," he said.
Another obstacle to greater independence for Russian metal producers is international raw material producers' reluctance to sell to cash-strapped Russian smelters.
"A lot of mines are reluctant for Russian smelters to buy their concentrates," Kohli said.
In cases where western firms have actually bought stakes in Russian plants, severing tolling ties could be fatal.

"One factor is who owns shares in the plants. If it is a western trading company then there is no chance (of reducing dependence on tolling arrangements)," said a Moscow-based trader at a western metals firm.
London-based Trans-World Metals, Glencore AG of Switerland and others have big equity stakes in Russian aluminium smelters.
The Moscow trader said Russia's tax system favoured tolling over production and only a radical change to that system could help smelters buy and process their own ores.
"If the government said they wouldn't charge export taxes next year, then it might give them some chance," he said.
Generalov said on Wednesday the exporter group would appeal to President Boris Yeltsin to give producers tax and other breaks needed to stand on their own feet.
Tolling is most dominant in Russian aluminium, where it accounts for around 69 percent of output. But it also accounts for a major slice of zinc, lead and tin production.
Tolling has given major commodity traders like Glencore and Trans-World, who supply large tonnages of ores and concentrates to Russian smelters for refining, a golden niche.
But analysts said the two companies were also investing in Russian metals factories as part of a long-term strategy.

Other trading firms also toll in Russia, but their involvement is less constant, because it depends more on changes to concentrate and ore prices relative to refined metal values as well as refining and treatment charges, analysts said.
